items.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024
items.q: When Tony Williams takes a solo I mean it’s not pulse orientation, it’s phrase orientation.

ctx.x: Oh you know it’s funny I — sometimes what I do with that section instead of playing those exact notes we’ll play random pitches [scats] and I mean it’s one of those things where really great drummers in this field, people like Dafnis Prieto or my son Zachary O’Farrill, are able to think in polyrhythmic ways. So in other words they’re hearing clave, they’re hearing the pulse, they’re also hearing the phrase. And so they’re hearing in three, they’re hearing in two, they’re hearing in six. And so they’re able to,…

eight measures later. Because they’re able to hear. And that’s really to me, that’s a very African way of approaching music. When you think about the cross stick rhythms of Ghana and the different djembe rhythms in Africa you realize that they work on multiple levels. They work in two, they work in three, they work in six, they work in these larger entities that are musical phrases which is amazing to me because sometimes in the hands of the right people, in the hands of Tony Williams, you can also hear this in…
I have to say it’s funny that you say that because to me that was very sophisticated.
